title: How Should Intelligent Tutoring Systems Sequence Multiple Graphical Representations of Fractions? A Multi-Methods Study
extended_summary:
This paper asks how intelligent tutoring systems should sequence multiple graphical representations of fractions to best support learning. The central question is whether representations should be blocked, fully interleaved, moderately interleaved, or increasingly interleaved across problems, and whether any observed advantage is driven mainly by reactivation of prior knowledge or by abstraction across representations.

The authors study the Fractions Tutor, an intelligent tutoring system for 4th- and 5th-grade fractions instruction that uses interactive circle, rectangle, and number line representations. In the main classroom experiment, 230 students from six schools in Western Pennsylvania were randomly assigned to one of four representation-sequencing conditions while keeping task-type sequencing moderately interleaved across all groups. Students completed pretests, immediate posttests, and delayed posttests; outcomes included reproduction with area models, reproduction with number lines, conceptual transfer, and procedural transfer. The paper also includes a small think-aloud study with six 5th-grade students and a log-data analysis using Bayesian knowledge tracing to probe the mechanisms behind any effects.

Overall, students improved from pretest to posttest across conditions, showing that the tutor supported learning. Evidence for an advantage of interleaving graphical representations was qualified but suggestive: the fully interleaved condition performed best on some outcomes, especially delayed conceptual transfer, and interleaving was particularly beneficial for students with low prior knowledge. The think-aloud data suggested that students did not spontaneously make many connections between representations unless prompted, supporting reactivation more than abstraction as the main mechanism. The authors conclude that interleaving representations can improve robust learning in an ITS for fractions, but that the best schedule may depend on learners' prior knowledge and the target knowledge type.
quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed classroom experiment with random assignment to four conditions and hierarchical linear modeling, so it has substantial credibility. It is not blue because it is not a full meta-analysis and there are some design/interpretation limits, including a modest sample in the final analytic sample and only partial/conditional effects.
impact_tier_rationale: The intervention produced modest but meaningful gains on some fraction outcomes, with effect sizes in the small-to-moderate range (e.g., d=0.33 on delayed conceptual transfer and up to d=0.75 on delayed number-line reproduction within the fully interleaved condition). The impact is positive but not uniformly large across all outcomes or schedules.

interventions.use_case: fractions tutoring with step-by-step guidance, hints, and multiple interactive graphical representations (circles, rectangles, number lines) for 4th- and 5th-grade learners; the study manipulates the sequencing of representations within the tutor

finding.finding_summary: In a classroom experiment with 230 4th- and 5th-grade students, all conditions improved from pretest to posttest on several fraction outcomes, including reproduction with area models (e.g., fully interleaved post>pre d=0.45; delayed>pre d=0.38), reproduction with number lines (e.g., fully interleaved post>pre d=0.51; delayed>pre d=0.75), and conceptual transfer (e.g., fully interleaved post>pre d=0.34; delayed>pre d=0.60). However, the advantage of interleaving over blocking was limited and heterogeneous: the fully interleaved condition significantly outperformed the other conditions on delayed conceptual transfer (d=0.33), while the increasingly interleaved condition showed a marginal advantage on reproduction with area models (d=0.30).
finding.measure: Fraction knowledge tests: reproduction with area models, reproduction with number lines, conceptual transfer, and procedural transfer
finding.effect_size: d=0.33 to d=0.75 (depending on condition and outcome)

finding.finding_summary: The paper’s broader instructional focus also included conceptual transfer and robust learning, which are proxies for deeper reasoning and the ability to apply fraction knowledge to novel tasks. The strongest evidence was for delayed conceptual transfer, where the fully interleaved condition significantly outperformed the other schedules (d=0.33), suggesting better long-term application of knowledge rather than only short-term practice performance.
finding.measure: Conceptual transfer items and delayed posttest performance
